page: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard.E4.Flex.32-128 is an x86_64 compute-focused virtual machine instance powered by an AMD EPYC 7J13 processor operating at a base clock frequency of 2.55 GHz. The instance configuration provisions 32 dedicated physical cores and 64 vCPUs via two threads per core, backed by 128 GB of total system memory. This sizing establishes a strict 1:2 vCPU-to-RAM ratio, allocating 2.0 GB of memory per execution thread.

The instance does not include integrated local NVMe storage or hardware GPU accelerators, necessitating network-attached block volumes for persistent filesystem operations. Dedicated CPU core assignment eliminates resource contention and hypervisor throttling associated with shared-core or burstable configurations. Ingress and egress connectivity is supported by one complimentary public IPv4 address.

Because the resource profile favors high core counts over large memory allocations, it offers qualitative resource efficiency for parallel execution. The configuration is suitable for distributed web serving layers, continuous integration build matrices, batch transcoding, ETL processing, and parallel computational workloads that do not exceed the 128 GB memory boundary.
description: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard.E4.Flex.32-128 is a compute-focused x86_64 virtual machine featuring a 2.55 GHz AMD EPYC 7J13 processor. The configuration allocates 32 dedicated physical CPU cores supporting 64 vCPUs through simultaneous multithreading, paired with 128 GB of main memory. This yields a 1:2 vCPU-to-RAM ratio with 2.0 GB of memory per core. The instance lacks local ephemeral storage and GPU acceleration, requiring cloud block storage for persistent filesystem operations, and includes one complimentary public IPv4 address. Dedicated core allocation ensures consistent compute availability without hypervisor resource contention or burst-state limitations. With substantial parallel processing capacity and a lean per-thread memory footprint, the instance is suitable for high-concurrency web serving, distributed batch computations, code compilation pipelines, and CPU-intensive data transformations.
